DEC-262 (a9), read by ref (quest decision view DEC-262 in opum-doc), relayed verbatim by the leader. Q1 tpm2-tools with three conditions: (i) key material only on pipes (the vault key into tpm2_create on stdin with -i -, out of tpm2_unseal on stdout, read by Ward directly; never in argv, a temp file or the environment; only sealed public and private blobs and contexts touch disk, in Ward's 0700 directory); (ii) the unseal runs in an encrypted (salted HMAC) session, and if the installed tpm2-tools cannot do that the slice comes back to opum-doc; (iii) detect the capability by presence, not version: missing tpm2-tools or no /dev/tpmrm0 access refuses by name, fail-closed, naming what to install or which group to join; supported hosts need the tpm2-tools package and the ADR says so. libtss2 via FFI is the fallback only on opum-doc's ruling, never on my own. Q2 no PCR binding; the ADR states the threat model plainly: it protects against copying the blob off the host and against other non-root users, not against root or an attacker who boots that machine. Q3 the 32-byte vault key itself is sealed; the vault format is unchanged (DEC-255 a6). Slices 0-5 approved as proposed.
THE TWO BINDING SLICE-2 POINTS, verbatim: "(1) A fresh salted session for every unseal, never a reused s.ctx, whatever 5b showed. And slice 2 must show `tpm2_sessionconfig` reporting decrypt/encrypt on the session it uses, as a pass/fail check in its tests' measurement and in T26. If parameter encryption reads off, that's the AC2 stop." and "(2) Ward sets and verifies 0600 itself on every blob and context file it writes. The 0660 s.ctx under umask 077 proves the tools' own modes can't be trusted. A file found wider than 0600 is the "blob not user-private" state, and refuses." Slice 2's tests: fake tpm2_* executables on a controlled PATH record argv, environment and stdin, and the tests scan the working directory afterwards, proving the key bytes appear only on stdin and stdout; refusal tests for tpm2-tools missing and /dev/tpmrm0 absent or unreadable, by name. The limit stays stated: this proves what Ward passes to the tools, not what the real tools do with the TPM; only T26 does.

JETSON, read-only measurements (launcher /Users/jdnewhouse/.scripts/jetson, an ssh wrapper; never read or print its key). tpm2-tools 5.6 (tpm2_unseal --version: tool="tpm2_unseal" version="5.6" tctis="libtss2-tctildr" tcti-default=tcti-device). Man pages read: tpm2_startauthsession -c, --key-context "Set the tpmkey and bind objects to be the same. Session parameter encryption is turned on. Session parameter decryption is turned on."; tpm2_create "-i -" reads stdin ("If file is -, read from stdin"), sealed data up to 128 bytes; tpm2_unseal -o "Defaults to STDOUT if not specified"; the tpm2_sessionconfig example calls "startauthsession ... -c prim.ctx" a "bounded & salted session". The bounded throwaway probe (forced TPM2TOOLS_TCTI=device:/dev/tpmrm0, 32 random throwaway bytes, transient objects only, mode-0700 dir deleted afterwards, handles identical before and after): a session started in one process and used by a second process worked (-S s.ctx), the same session file reused for a second unseal also worked, and -p session:<file> worked; all four unseals printed the throwaway's sha256 (a2897eac3a3d2e3f1a76a54831567da3559a72823caf5a9535cf89fb056d22cb). The fresh login had group tss and /dev/tpmrm0 is crw-rw---- tss:tss. THREE THINGS IT DID NOT PROVE: (1) that the unsealed bytes were encrypted on the TPM interface (use tpm2_sessionconfig on the session file, read-only, in slice 2's measurement); (2) anything beyond one host, one tpm2-tools build, one run, and no reboot (T26 does that); (3) whether the man page's "cannot be saved/loaded again" holds, since reuse worked here; hence the binding rule of a fresh session per unseal. Also measured: tpm2-tools wrote s.ctx 0660 despite umask 077, which is the basis for binding point (2). The operator confirmed the jetson host step (user in group tss) and the jetson T26 run. spark has no TPM2 and stays unsupported by presence. No binary has been copied to jetson, no reboot done.

BLOCKING (finding 1): the race test passes against the old O_EXCL fallback too. The old fallback overlapped only through its reaping path (B reads holder A's pid, A releases and exits, C takes the lock, B finds A dead and removes C's file, then takes a second lock). My probes are long-lived loopers that always release before exiting, so no dead recorded pid exists and the reaping path is unreachable; the no-lock control is a weaker baseline than the old fallback. FIX SHAPE: each round, spawn a batch of fresh one-shot processes behind a start barrier; each takes the lock once, holds it, releases and exits, so dead recorded pids exist every round; optionally seed setup.lock with a dead pid and have some holders exit or be killed while holding; 20 or more rounds, same O_EXCL marker detector, keep the no-lock control; and RECORD ONE MEASUREMENT of that harness against the parent 316f566 (platform faked for that one run only) showing overlaps > 0, so the test is proven able to fail on the thing it replaces. The barrier also removes the flake risk of finding 6 (expect denied > 0 assumes the 4 probes overlap in time).

FINDING 7 (O_CLOEXEC versus a spawned tpm2-tools inheriting the lock fd) goes into WCLI-21 slice 2's design: the lock lives on the open file description, so a child spawned while it is held shares it if the fd lacks close-on-exec and keeps it held after the parent exits (liveness, not safety).
